_note: The causal map — 'what this moves'. Hand-written, deterministic, no model involved. Rendered as plain-English lines under each metric so a student can see how one number reaches another. 'dir' is the usual direction when the source rises.

affects.because: Bunker fuel is refined from crude, so marine fuel prices follow Brent with a short lag.
On a voyage charter the owner pays for the fuel, so dearer bunkers cut daily earnings even when the freight rate hasn't moved.
Brent rising faster than WTI widens the gap, which is what makes exporting US crude profitable.

links.watch_for: A common beginner's trap is assuming high oil prices are good for tankers. They aren't by themselves — tankers are paid to move barrels a distance, not to move expensive barrels. What matters is volume and voyage length.

affects.because: A wide gap pulls US crude to Asia and Europe. Those are long voyages, so each cargo ties up a ship for far longer.

links.watch_for: Think in tonne-miles, not tonnes. The same barrel shipped twice as far doubles the work the fleet has to do.

affects.because: Fuel is the largest voyage cost, so it comes straight off the owner's TCE.
The same arithmetic applies to bulkers on voyage charters.

links.watch_for: Scrubber-fitted ships are affected differently — they burn cheaper high-sulphur fuel, so a wide VLSFO-to-IFO380 spread actually works in their favour.

affects.because: What matters is not the level but the gap to Asian JKM prices. The wider gap decides which way cargoes sail, and therefore how far they travel.
Expensive gas pushes European power stations back towards coal, lifting coal imports and the bulkers that carry them.

links.watch_for: European gas prices reach dry bulk through fuel switching in power generation. It's a good example of how two apparently unrelated markets connect.

affects.because: Cheap US gas relative to Europe and Asia is what makes US LNG exports profitable, and those long-haul cargoes are what LNG carriers depend on. Expensive US gas narrows the arbitrage and can idle export capacity.
US gas processing produces the propane that VLGCs carry from the US Gulf to Asia.

links.watch_for: For LNG and LPG shipping, the spread between regions matters far more than any single price.

affects.because: Coal is one of the two main Capesize and Panamax cargoes, so stronger coal trade means more large bulker demand.
Capesize and Panamax earnings are the heaviest components of the index.

links.watch_for: Where coal comes from matters as much as how much moves. Colombian coal to Europe is a far shorter voyage than Australian coal to Europe.

affects.because: Fat margins make refineries run at full tilt, producing more diesel and gasoline that needs shipping.
Strong margins also support the long-haul product cargoes that large product tankers carry.
Refineries running hard need more crude delivered to them in the first place.

links.watch_for: This is the best leading indicator for clean tanker rates. Refinery economics drive cargo volumes before freight rates react.

affects.because: The ETF holds dry bulk freight futures, which settle against Baltic indices, so it tracks the index closely.

links.watch_for: The BDI is often reported as a gauge of world trade. Be careful: it reflects the balance between cargo and the number of ships available. A falling BDI can mean a flood of newbuildings rather than weak demand — always check the orderbook before drawing conclusions.

affects.because: Capesize earnings carry the largest weight in the index and are its most volatile part.

links.watch_for: Capesize rates are essentially a bet on Chinese steel production, because iron ore dominates the cargo.

affects.because: When the largest tankers get expensive, charterers split cargoes into smaller ships, pulling Suezmax rates up behind them.

links.watch_for: The tanker classes are substitutes at the margin, so strength usually spreads from one size to the next rather than staying contained.

affects.because: The crack is the product price minus crude, so stronger diesel widens it directly.
Distillate strength pulls refinery output away from residual fuel, tightening the marine fuel pool.

links.watch_for: Diesel is the product most tied to industrial activity and freight, so it tends to lead the wider fuel complex.
